paragraph: Lakshmana shook with an uncontrollable rage. He stomped around with flailing arms flashing eyes and stormy demeanor, making him seem like an intoxicated tusker. To this fiery embodiment of fury, whose sighs sounded like the hissing of king cobras Rama quietly said: "Lakshmana! Your anger against our father and your sorrow for me has to be restrained. The coronation has not been stopped for any lack of competence on your part, so it is of no disgrace to you. Do show the same zeal in procuring things for my exile, as you did for my coronation. As for mother Kausalya, I rely on you to dispel her doubts about my ever becoming ruler of Ayodhya. It grieves me to see her agonizing over me, but the king will be distressed if his promises are violated. His distress will also be mine. My early departure will make queen Kaikeyi happy and clear the way for Bharata's installation."
Situation/Problem_Faced: Lakshmana is in an uncontrollable rage due to Rama's impending exile and the perceived injustice to Rama and Kausalya. Rama, with calm composure, addresses Lakshmana's anger and sorrow, explaining the necessity of his exile to uphold his father's promises and ensure the happiness of Kaikeyi and Bharata's coronation. Rama also entrusts Lakshmana with the responsibility of comforting Kausalya.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Rama exemplifies emotional regulation and selflessness in this passage. He prioritizes his father's honor and the well-being of the kingdom over his personal desires and suffering. He calmly guides Lakshmana towards acceptance and service, redirecting his brother's intense emotions towards constructive action. This demonstrates Rama's commitment to Dharma (righteous duty) and his ability to lead even in adversity.
Outcome/Resolution: In this specific exchange, Rama successfully de-escalates Lakshmana's rage by calmly appealing to his sense of duty and rationale. He redirects Lakshmana's intense emotions from thoughts of violence and defiance toward accepting the exile and providing support to Kausalya and the King. This interaction marks a significant step in Lakshmana's acceptance of Rama's path and his commitment to aiding him, leading to a shift from conflict to shared purpose.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.anger Management: Emotional control, composure, self-restraint, managing fury, impulse control
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.stress Management: Coping mechanisms, resilience,emotional coping, distress tolerance

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Dharma (Righteous duty; Rama's adherence to his father's word)
Tyaga (Sacrifice; Rama's willingness to go into exile for his father's promise)
Seva (Service; Rama entrusting Lakshmana with comforting Kausalya and aiding in exile preparations)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The passage deeply explores 'Dharma' through Rama's unwavering commitment to his father's promise, a form of 'Tyaga' (sacrifice). It contrasts Lakshmana's 'Krodha' (anger) and 'Shoka' (sorrow) with Rama's 'Sthitaprajna' (steadfast wisdom) and his calm approach to managing the situation. Rama also assigns Lakshmana to 'Seva' (service) by asking him to comfort Kausalya.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, this passage vividly portrays anger management and emotional regulation through the stark contrast between Lakshmana's uncontrolled rage and Rama's remarkable composure. It highlights the pervasive low mood and sadness within the family due to the impending exile. The narrative is driven by significant relationship challenges, with Rama actively working to mitigate conflict and guide emotional responses. Rama's calm demeanor in the face of adversity also demonstrates effective stress management and a profound sense of empathy towards his family members, even as he adheres to his duty.
